text: Through love, bitter turns sweet and *copper turns to gold*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book II, story of Luqman (Ganjoor II §31, couplet 20; c. II.1529–30 in Nicholson)
original: از محبت تلخ‌ها شیرین شود / از محبت مس‌ها زرین شود

text: Lord, if I worship you from fear of hell, burn me in it; if from hope of paradise, deny it to me. If I worship you *for your own sake*, do not hide your lasting beauty from me.
author: Rabia al-Adawiyya
ref: reported by Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on Rabia
original: خداوندا اگر تو را از بیم دوزخ می‌پرستم در دوزخم بسوز و اگر به امید بهشت می‌پرستم بر من حرام گردان و اگر برای تو تو را می‌پرستم جمال باقی دریغ مدار
note: Attar wrote this down in Persian about four centuries after Rabia. Nothing in her own hand survives.

text: I did not come to quarrel; my work is love. The Friend lives in hearts, and I came *to build hearts*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem with the couplet “Ben gelmedim dava için” (Tatcı ed., poem 179, couplet 2)
original: Ben gelmedim dava için, benim işim sevi için / Dostun evi gönüllerdir, gönüller yapmaya geldim
note: “The Friend” (Dost) is God.

text: Whoever's heart has been brought alive by love *will never die*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 11 (Qazvini-Ghani numbering, as on Ganjoor), couplet beginning “هرگز نمیرد”
original: هرگز نمیرد آن که دلش زنده شد به عشق
note: The couplet goes on: “our permanence is recorded in the ledger of the world”.

text: I follow the religion of love: wherever its camels turn, *love is my religion* and my faith.
author: Ibn Arabi
ref: poem XI, verse 15
original: أدين بدين الحب أنى توجهت ركائبه فالحب ديني وإيماني

text: Loves that chase a pretty color are *not love at all*; in the end they are only a disgrace.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the king and the handmaid (Ganjoor I §9, couplet 21)
original: عشق‌هایی کز پی رنگی بود / عشق نبود عاقبت ننگی بود
note: “Color” means outward looks: in the story, a love fades as the beloved’s beauty does.

text: Plant the tree of friendship: it bears the heart's desire. *Uproot the sapling of enmity*: it bears endless pain.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 115 (Ganjoor numbering), opening couplet
original: درختِ دوستی بنشان که کامِ دل به بار آرد / نهالِ دشمنی بَرکَن که رنج بی‌شمار آرد

text: It is love: keep your heart out of it, for *passion is no easy thing*. No one it has worn away chose it with his reason intact.
author: Ibn al-Farid
ref: ode beginning “Huwa al-hubbu fa-slam bi’l-hasha”, verse 1
original: هو الحب فاسلم بالحشا ما الهوى سهل فما اختاره مضنى به وله عقل
note: The opening line of one of his best-known odes.

text: Do not be without love, or you will be dead. *Die in love*, and stay alive.
author: Rumi
ref: quatrain 1600 (Ganjoor numbering), second couplet
original: بی‌عشق مباش تا نباشی مرده / در عشق بمیر تا بمانی زنده

text: Do not look for *a flawless beloved*: you will not find one.
author: Abu Sa'id Abu'l-Khayr
ref: reported by Muhammad ibn Munawwar, Asrar al-Tawhid, ch. 2, part 3, sayings no. 8
original: معشوقۀ بی‌عیب مجویید که نیابید.

text: Here love is fire and *reason is smoke*: when love arrives, reason quickly runs away.
author: Attar
ref: the Valley of Love (Mantiq al-Tayr)
original: عشق اینجا آتشست و عقل دود / عشق کامد در گریزد عقل زود
note: The second of the seven valleys the birds must cross to reach the Simurgh.

text: Love is to count as little the much you give, and *the little your beloved gives* as much.
author: Bayazid Bistami
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on love (bab al-mahabba)
original: المحبة استقلال الكثير من نفسك، واستكثار القليل من حبيبك

text: Saying Ranjha, Ranjha, I have *become Ranjha myself*. Call me Ranjha now; let no one call me Heer.
author: Bulleh Shah
ref: kafi “Rānjhā rānjhā kardī nī maiṅ āpe rānjhā hoī”
original: رانجھا رانجھا کردی نی میں آپے رانجھا ہوئی ۔ / سدو نی مینوں دھیدو رانجھا، ہیر نہ آکھو کوئی ۔
note: Heer and Ranjha are the great lovers of Punjabi legend. Bulleh speaks as Heer.

text: Hoping to rise high by piling up learning was an impossible wish. *Love is all there is*; learning is only talk.
author: Fuzuli
ref: kıta beginning “İlm kesbiyle pâye-i rif’at” (Akyüz et al. ed., p. 306)
original: İlm kesbiyle pâye-i rif’at / Ârzû-yı muhâl imiş ancak / Aşk imiş her ne var âlemde / İlm bir kîl ü kâl imiş ancak

text: Of all the keepsakes left beneath this turning dome, I found none sweeter than *the sound of love's words*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 178 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: از صدایِ سخنِ عشق ندیدم خوشتر / یادگاری که در این گنبدِ دَوّار بِمانْد
note: The “turning dome” is the sky, and so the world.

text: Whoever has not died in love has not lived by it. *Before the honey* come the stings of the bees.
author: Ibn al-Farid
ref: ode beginning “Huwa al-hubbu fa-slam bi’l-hasha”, verse 6
original: فمن لم يمت في حبه لم يعش به، ودون اجتناء النحل ما جنت النحل
note: In Sufi poetry, to die in love is to die to the self.

text: Every love that rests on a motive *ends when the motive ends*.
author: Junayd of Baghdad
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on love (bab al-mahabba)
original: كل محبة كانت لغرض إذا زال الغرض زالت تلك المحبة

text: Strive to *hold the hem of love*: love will make you pure. Heart, never lose heart.
author: Kaygusuz Abdal
ref: poem 235, couplet 5 (Güzel ed.)
original: Cehd eyle hemân aşk eteğine elin ersin / Aşk sâfi kılar seni gönül hiç melâl olma

text: Go and sweep *the house of the heart*; make it ready for the Beloved. When you step out, He steps in.
author: Mahmud Shabistari
ref: section 25
original: برو تو خانهٔ دل را فرو روب / مهیّا کن مقام و جای محبوب / چو تو بیرون شدی او اندر آید / به تو، بی تو جمالِ خود نماید

text: I was dead and came alive; I was weeping and turned to laughter. *Love’s fortune came*, and I became a fortune that lasts.
author: Rumi
ref: ghazal 1393 (Ganjoor numbering), opening couplet
original: مرده بدم زنده شدم، گریه بدم خنده شدم / دولت عشق آمد و من دولت پاینده شدم

text: A friend won over a lifetime should not be hurt in a moment. A stone takes years to become a ruby: *do not shatter it* with one blow.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter VIII, maxim 55
original: دوستی را که به عمری فرا چنگ آرند، نشاید که به یک دم بیازارند. سنگی به چند سال شود لعل پاره‌ای / زنهار تا به یک نفسش نشکنی به سنگ
note: It was once believed that the sun, over many years, slowly ripened common stone into ruby.

text: If you would love, then do the work of love. Love’s road is the eye of a needle: *become a thread*, and you will pass.
author: Shah Hussain
ref: kafi “Āshiq hoveṅ tāṅ ishq kamāveṅ”
original: عاشق ہوویں تاں عشقَ کماویں ۔ / راہ عشقَ دا سوئی دا نکا، تاگا ہووے تاں جاویں ۔

text: A mustard seed’s weight of love is dearer to me than *seventy years of worship* without love.
author: Yahya ibn Mu'adh
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on love (bab al-mahabba)
original: مثقال خردلة من الحب أحب إلي من عبادة سبعين سنة بلا حب
note: Yahya of Rayy was known as “the Preacher”.

text: Listen, friends: love is like the sun. A heart that has no love is *like a stone*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “İşitin ey yârenler” (Tatcı ed., poem 66, couplet 1)
original: İşitin ey yârenler, aşk bir güneşe benzer / Aşkı olmayan gönül misâl-i taşa benzer

text: I gave my heart to the Friend, and love became my companion. From whoever will not give the Friend their heart, *love turns away*.
author: Ümmi Sinan
ref: Bilgin ed., poem 64, couplet 1
original: Ben ol dosta virdüm gönül aşk benüm ile yâr olur / Kim ki dosta virmez gönül bu aşk andan bîzâr olur
note: “The Friend” (Dost) is God.

text: Knowledge means knowing; knowledge means *knowing yourself*. If you do not know yourself, what is all your reading for?
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “İlim ilim bilmektir”
original: İlim ilim bilmektir, ilim kendin bilmektir / Sen kendini bilmezsin, ya nice okumaktır
note: Manuscripts vary in wording.

text: Nothing stands between the lover and the beloved. Hafez, *you are your own veil*: step out of the way.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 266 (Ganjoor numbering), closing couplet
original: میانِ عاشق و معشوق هیچ حائل نیست / تو خود حجابِ خودی حافظ از میان برخیز

text: Brother, *you are your thought*; the rest of you is bone and fiber. If your thought is a rose, you are a rose garden; if a thorn, you are fuel for the furnace.
author: Rumi
ref: Book II, v. 277–278 (Ganjoor II §9, couplets 35–36)
original: ای برادر تو همان اندیشه‌ای / ما بقی تو استخوان و ریشه‌ای / گر گلست اندیشهٔ تو گلشنی / ور بود خاری تو هیمهٔ گلخنی
note: Rumi glossed “thought” here as an inner awareness, not ordinary thinking (Fihi ma fihi, ch. 52).

text: The root of every wrong, every lapse and every craving is being pleased with yourself. The root of every good, every waking and every restraint is *not being pleased with yourself*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 33 at the source (35 in many editions)
original: أصل كل معصية وغفلة وشهوة الرضا عن النفس، وأصل كل طاعة ويقظة وعفة عدم الرضا منك عنها
note: The Hikam is numbered a little differently from one edition to the next.

text: For twelve years I was the blacksmith of my self. I laid it in the furnace of discipline, heated it in the fire of struggle, beat it with the hammer of blame, and *made a mirror of it*.
author: Bayazid Bistami
ref: reported by Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on Bayazid
original: دوازده سال آهنگر نفس خود بودم، در کوره ریاضت می‌نهادم و با آتش مجاهده می‌تافتم و بر سندان مذمت می‌نهادم و پتک ملامت بر او می‌زدم تا از نفس خویش آینه‌ای کردم
note: Shortened. The saying also has an anvil of reproach, and goes on with five more years of polishing the mirror.

text: *Look kindly at yourself*: you are the essence of the world.
author: Şeyh Galib
ref: refrain couplet of the terci-i bend “Ey dil ey dil niye bu rütbede pür-gamsın sen”
original: Hoşça bak zâtına kim zübde-i âlemsin sen
note: The couplet goes on: “you are the human being who is the pupil of creation’s eye”. Galib was the Mevlevi sheikh of Galata.

text: You held blue glass before your eyes, so the whole world looked blue. Unless you are blind, *know the blue is yours*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the lion sees himself in the well (Ganjoor I §72, couplets 26–27)
original: پیش چشمت داشتی شیشهٔ کبود / زان سبب عالم کبودت می‌نمود / گر نه کوری این کبودی دان ز خویش / خویش را بد گو مگو کس را تو بیش
note: The couplet goes on: “speak ill of yourself, not of others”.

text: Eloquence belongs to the heart, not the tongue. Weep for yourself a thousand times, and *for others once*.
author: Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani
ref: session (majlis) 51, p. 213 of the Cairo edition
original: الفصاحة للقلب لا للسان، ابك على نفسك ألفا وعلى غيرك مرة
note: Al-Fath al-Rabbani records the sermons he gave in Baghdad in 1150–51.

text: Each one was made for some work, and *the longing for it* was set in their heart.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, the hermit on the mountain (Ganjoor III §68, couplet 5)
original: هر کسی را بهر کاری ساختند / میل آن را در دلش انداختند

text: Lord, keep Abdullah from three plagues: the whisperings of the devil, the cravings of the self, and *the pride of ignorance*.
author: Abdullah Ansari of Herat
ref: Munajat-i Pir-i Ansar, no. 87 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: الهی عبدالله را از سه آفت نگاه دار از وسواس شیطانی و خواهشهای نفسانی و غرور نادانی
note: Abdullah is Ansari himself.

text: While you seek a jewel from the mine, you are a mine; while you crave a scrap of bread, you are bread. *Whatever you seek, you are*.
author: Rumi
ref: quatrain 1815 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: تا در طلب گوهر کانی کانی / تا در هوس لقمهٔ نانی نانی / این نکتهٔ رمز اگر بدانی دانی / هر چیز که در جستن آنی آنی

text: How long will you fret over bread and clothes, over what people say of you? With so much useless worrying *you have worn yourself out*.
author: Attar
ref: discourse 12, opening section
original: ترا اندوه نان و جامه تا کی‌؟ / ترا از نام و ننگ عامه تا کی‌؟ / ز بس که‌اندیشهٔ بیهوده کردی / نهاد خویش را فرسوده کردی

text: Farid, if you have a fine mind, do not write black marks against others. Bow your head and *look into your own collar*.
author: Baba Farid
work: Shaloks in the Guru Granth Sahib
ref: Salok Sheikh Farid 6, Ang 1378
original: ਫਰੀਦਾ ਜੇ ਤੂ ਅਕਲਿ ਲਤੀਫੁ ਕਾਲੇ ਲਿਖੁ ਨ ਲੇਖ ॥ / ਆਪਨੜੇ ਗਿਰੀਵਾਨ ਮਹਿ ਸਿਰੁ ਨਂੀਵਾਂ ਕਰਿ ਦੇਖੁ ॥੬॥
note: To look into your own collar is to examine yourself.

text: The people with the most worries are *those with the worst character*.
author: Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on character (bab al-khuluq)
original: من أكثر الناس هما؟ قال: أسوأهم خلقا
note: His answer when asked who carries the most care.

text: Look into your heart and know who you are: whoever *sees himself in the heart* has woken up.
author: Erzurumlu İbrahim Hakkı
ref: Divan, no. 106 in the edition cited
original: Kalbine eyle nazar, kendini tanı kimsin / Kendüyi dilde gören ehl-i dil âgâh olmuş

text: Put up with everyone, yes: everyone *except your own self*.
author: Hatim al-Asamm
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on character (bab al-khuluq)
original: أيحتمل الرجل من كل أحد، فقال: نعم إلا من نفسه
note: His answer when asked whether a person should bear with everyone. Hatim was called “the Deaf”.

text: Looking into *the faults hidden in you* is better than peering into the mysteries hidden from you.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 30 at the source
original: تشوفك إلى ما بطن فيك من العيوب خير من تشوفك إلى ما حجب عنك من الغيوب
note: The Arabic rhymes: ʿuyūb (faults), ghuyūb (hidden things).

text: Do not boast that you are free of pride: it is harder to see than *an ant's footprint* on black stone on a dark night.
author: Jami
ref: First Garden (on the Sufi masters), section 7
original: لاف بی کبری مزن کان از نشان پای مور / در شب تاریک بر سنگ سیه پنهان‌تر است
note: Jami goes on: digging up a mountain with a needle is easier than getting pride out of yourself.

text: Go, my friend, and know yourself well: *a swelling is not fat*.
author: Mahmud Shabistari
ref: section 15, the answer on what “I” is
original: برو ای خواجه خود را نیک بشناس / که نبوَد فربهی مانند آماس
note: Self-importance can pass for growth, as a swelling can pass for health.

text: When the mirror shows your face truly, *break yourself*, not the mirror: breaking the mirror is the wrong.
author: Nizami
ref: section 47, tale of the unjust king and the truthful man
original: آینه چون نقش تو بنمود راست / خود شکن آیینه شکستن خطاست
note: Said to a tyrant by the one man who dared tell him the truth.

text: If you would make something clean, clean *the house of your heart*. What is water for, if you only wash your face?
author: Pir Sultan Abdal
ref: Aslanoğlu ed., poem 65, stanza 1
original: Arıdırsan kalbin evini arıt / Yüzünü yumağa suyu n’eylersin
note: Pir Sultan’s poems survive in song-books and oral tradition, and several poets used his name.

text: If a king sends you to a village on one errand, and you do a hundred other things but not that one, *you have done nothing*.
author: Rumi
ref: chapter 3
original: همچنانکه پادشاهی تو را به ده فرستاد برای کاری معین، تو رفتی و صد کار دیگر گزاردی چون آن کار را که برای آن رفته بودی نگزاردی چنان است که هیچ نگزاردی.
note: Rumi goes on: each of us came into this world for one task, and that task is the point.

text: The heart is a river *deeper than the seas*: who can know what hearts hold? Inside it are boats and quarrels, oars and boatmen.
author: Sultan Bahu
ref: bait “Dil daryā samundron ḍūnghe” (no. 63 in the Punjabi Kavita text)
original: دل دریا سمندروں ڈونگھے، کون دلاں دیاں جانے ہو ۔ / وچے بیڑے وچے جھیڑے، وچے ونجھ مہانے ہو ۔
note: Every line of Bahu’s verses ends on “hu”, a breath that is also a name of God.

text: Waris Shah, *habits never leave*, even if you cut a person apart joint by joint.
author: Waris Shah
ref: stanza 280, the yogi’s answer to Ranjha
original: وارث شاہ نہ عادتاں جاندیاں نے، بھانویں کٹیئے پوریاں پوریاں وو ۔
note: In the poem a yogi says this to Ranjha, who has come to him to become a mendicant.

text: Alas, heart, you have scattered yourself across the world. What have you gained by *never being still*?
author: Ümmi Sinan
ref: Bilgin ed., poem 95, couplet 1
original: Ey dirîgâ sen seni hep âleme yaydun gönül / Böyle her dem bî-karâr olmakda ne tuydun gönül

text: When your heart tightens, *see the opening inside it*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, Mary and the Holy Spirit (Ganjoor III §179, couplet 40; c. III.3726–3739)
original: چونک قبض آید تو در وی بسط بین
note: The couplet goes on: “stay fresh, and do not knit your brow”. Qabz and bast, tightening and opening, are Sufi terms for the heart’s contraction and expansion.

text: Patience is *swallowing bitterness* without a frown.
author: Junayd of Baghdad
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on patience (bab al-sabr)
original: الصبر تجرع المرارة من غير تعبيس
note: His answer when asked what patience is.

text: Lost Joseph will come back to Canaan: do not grieve. The house of sorrow will one day be a rose garden: *do not grieve*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 255, opening couplet
original: یوسف گم گشته بازآید به کنعان غم مخور / کلبهٔ احزان شود روزی گلستان غم مخور
note: Jacob grieved for his lost son Joseph in the “house of sorrows” until Joseph came back.

text: God turns ills into good; do not think He does otherwise. The wise only watch: let us see what the Lord will do. *Whatever He does, He does well*.
author: Erzurumlu İbrahim Hakkı
ref: opening stanza (also in his Marifetnâme)
original: Hak şerleri hayr eyler / Zannetme ki gayr eyler / Ârif anı seyr eyler / Mevlâ görelim neyler / Neylerse güzel eyler
note: Tefvîz means handing one’s affairs over to God.

text: I sought a cure for my pain: *my pain was the cure*.
author: Niyazi Mısri
ref: ghazal beginning “Derman arardım derdime”
original: Derman arardım derdime, derdim bana derman imiş
note: Still sung as a hymn (ilahi).

text: If every blow fills you with resentment, how will you ever become a mirror, *without being polished*?
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the Prophet’s counsel to Ali (Ganjoor I §140, couplet 22)
original: ور بهر زخمی تو پر کینه شوی / پس کجا بی‌صیقل آیینه شوی
note: Mirrors were polished metal; they shone only after hard rubbing.

text: If you are a lover, learn to bear trouble. Look at the oyster: through its affliction it turns a drop into *a pearl*.
author: Eşrefoğlu Rumi
ref: ghazal 27, couplet 6 (Güneş ed.)
original: Sen Eşrefoğlu Rûmî âşıkısan belâ-keş ol / Gör sadefi ki belâyıla katre’i gevher kılur
note: An old belief held that pearls grew from raindrops caught by oysters.

text: God created a hundred thousand elixirs, but no one has ever seen *an elixir like patience*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, Luqman and David (Ganjoor III §81, couplet 13)
original: صد هزاران کیمیا حق آفرید / کیمیایی همچو صبر آدم ندید
note: An elixir, in alchemy, was the substance that turned base metal into gold.

text: Give yourself *rest from scheming*: what Another has already taken on for you, do not take on yourself.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 4 at the source
original: أرح نفسك من التدبير، فما قام به غيرك لا تقم به لنفسك
note: “Another” is God.

text: Knock at a door, and in the end someone comes out. Dig at a well *every day*, and at last you reach clear water.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, the lover finds the beloved (Ganjoor III §228, couplets 3 and 5)
original: گفت پیغامبر که چون کوبی دری / عاقبت زان در برون آید سری / چون ز چاهی می‌کنی هر روز خاک / عاقبت اندر رسی در آب پاک
note: Rumi gives the first line as a saying of the Prophet.

text: Keep to patience, patience, and you will be held dear. If you wait with patience, *you will find meaning*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: section on anger and patience (Tatcı ed., p. 85)
original: Sabır gözet sabır azîz olasın / Sabır beklerisen ma’nî bulasın
note: The Risaletü’n-Nushiyye, “Treatise of Counsel,” is his long poem of advice, finished in 1307.

text: People suffer because they *want things before their time*.
author: Abu Sa'id Abu'l-Khayr
ref: reported by Muhammad ibn Munawwar, Asrar al-Tawhid, ch. 2, part 3, sayings no. 38
original: خلق از آن در رنجند کی کارها پیش از وقت می‌طلبند.

text: Whoever deserves to have fire poured on him and *gets off with ashes* has no right to be angry.
author: Abu Uthman al-Hiri
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on character (bab al-khuluq)
original: من استحق أن يصب عليه النار فصولح على الرماد لم يجز له أن يغضب
note: Said to his angry companions after someone emptied a basin of ashes on him from a rooftop.

text: Where there is a thorn there is basil too; where there is pain, *there is a cure*. If the cure is hidden today, it will show in its hour.
author: Attar
ref: discourse 11, opening section
original: چو خاری هست ریحان نیز باشد / چو دردی هست درمان نیز باشد / اگر امروز ظاهر نیست درمان / شود ظاهر چو آید وقت فرمان

text: Make patience your purpose and hold to it firmly. Then you will *grow into a river*, and never dwindle into a little stream.
author: Baba Farid
work: Shaloks in the Guru Granth Sahib
ref: Salok Sheikh Farid 117, Ang 1384
original: ਸਬਰੁ ਏਹੁ ਸੁਆਉ ਜੇ ਤੂੰ ਬੰਦਾ ਦਿੜੁ ਕਰਹਿ ॥ / ਵਧਿ ਥੀਵਹਿ ਦਰੀਆਉ ਟੁਟਿ ਨ ਥੀਵਹਿ ਵਾਹੜਾ ॥੧੧੭॥

text: Be patient like Job and *make no complaint* of your pain: love’s hunter catches nothing but trouble.
author: Eşrefoğlu Rumi
ref: ghazal 41, couplet 8 (Güneş ed.)
original: Eyyûb gibi sabr eyle derdüne kılma şikâyet / Işk avcısına belâdan özge şikâr ele girmez

text: Do not be hurt by the autumn wind in the garden of time. Think sensibly: where is *a rose without thorns*?
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 19 (Ganjoor numbering), closing couplet
original: حافظ از بادِ خزان در چمنِ دَهر مَرَنج / فکرِ معقول بفرما گُلِ بی‌خار کجاست؟

text: Sometimes He gives and so withholds; sometimes He withholds and so gives. Understand a refusal, and *the refusal becomes the gift*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 77 at the source
original: ربما أعطاك فمنعك، وربما منعك فأعطاك، ومتى فتح لك باب الفهم في المنع صار المنع عين العطاء

text: You are truly content when *misfortune pleases you* as much as blessing does.
author: Rabia al-Adawiyya
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on contentment (bab al-rida)
original: متى يكون العبد راضيا؟ فقالت: إذا سرته المصيبة كما سرته النعمة
note: Her answer when asked when a person can be called content.

text: For the moon’s sake, do not run from the night; for the rose and its scent, *put up with the thorn*.
author: Rumi
ref: quatrain 972 (Ganjoor numbering), second couplet
original: از بهر وصال ماه از شب مگریز / وز بهر گل و گلاب با خار بساز

text: Things come right through patience; the hasty fall headlong. In the desert I saw with my own eyes *the slow outrun the swift*.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter VIII, maxim 34
original: کارها به صبر بر آید و مُستَعجِل به سر در آید. به چشمِ خویش دیدم در بیابان / که آهسته سَبَق بُرد از شتابان

text: The rosebush that winter's cruelty has made look like firewood, wait: *spring's just hand* will bring it into bloom.
author: Sanai
ref: qasida 71 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: گلبنی کاکنون ترا هیزم نمود از جور دی / باش تا در جلوه‌ش آرد دست انصاف بهار

text: Look to the gentle and the forbearing; anger keeps company with sorrow. *Out of patience comes peace*, if you can understand it.
author: Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai
ref: Sur Yaman Kalyan, dastan 10, bait 13 (Bhittaipedia numbering)
original: نَمِي کَمِي نِھارِ تُون، ڏَمَرَ پاسي ڏُکُ، / مَنجهان صَبُرَ سُکُ، جَي سَنوارِئا سَمُجهين.

text: God made this world a place of hardship. Whoever truly comes into it must learn to *swallow its sorrows*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: Tatcı ed., poem 141, couplet 2
original: Çalab’ım bu dünyâyı kahır içün yaratmış / Gerçeğin gelenlerün kahrını yutmak gerek
note: Çalap is an old Turkish name for God.

text: A word can end a war; a word can cost a head. A word can turn *poisoned food to honey* and butter.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Keleci bilen kişinin yüzünü ak ede bir söz”
original: Söz ola kese savaşı, söz ola kestire başı / Söz ola ağulu aşı bal ile yağ ede bir söz

text: Until a man speaks, *his faults and gifts* stay hidden.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter I, story 3
original: تا مرد سخن نگفته باشد / عیب و هنرش نهفته باشد

text: Many an Indian and a Turk speak the same tongue; many two Turks are strangers to each other. *Being of one heart* is better than being of one tongue.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the hoopoe and Solomon (Ganjoor I §66, couplets 5–6; c. I.1206–07 in Nicholson)
original: ای بسا هندو و ترک همزبان / ای بسا دو ترک چون بیگانگان / پس زبان محرمی خود دیگرست / همدلی از همزبانی بهترست
note: One half-line between the two is left out: “the language of intimacy is something else”.

text: When talking pleases you, be silent; when silence pleases you, *speak*.
author: Bishr al-Hafi
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on silence (bab al-samt)
original: إذا أعجبك الكلام فاصمت، وإذا أعجبك الصمت فتكلم
note: Bishr “the Barefoot” of Baghdad.

text: Whoever keeps silent about the truth is *a mute devil*.
author: Abu Ali al-Daqqaq
ref: reported by Qushayri (his student), Risala, chapter on silence
original: من سكت عن الحق فهو شيطان أخرس
note: Qushayri heard it from Daqqaq, his teacher.

text: Silence is the sea, and speech is a stream. *The sea is seeking you*: do not go looking for the stream.
author: Rumi
ref: Book IV, the Prophet appoints a young commander (Ganjoor IV §77, couplet 33)
original: خامشی بحرست و گفتن هم‌چو جو / بحر می‌جوید ترا جو را مجو

text: Keep your hand from what is forbidden and *your tongue from backbiting*. Close up this shop before the hand of death reaches you.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: Tatcı ed., poem 35, couplet 4
original: Kesgil harâmdan elün, kesgil gaybetden dilün / Azrâîl el irmedin bu dükkânı dir gider
note: The original names Azrael, the angel of death.

text: Whoever keeps his secret soon has his wish. A seed hidden in the earth becomes *the green of the garden*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the king and the handmaid (Ganjoor I §7, couplets 33–34)
original: گفت پیغامبر که هر که سر نهفت / زود گردد با مراد خویش جفت / دانه چون اندر زمین پنهان شود / سر او سرسبزی بستان شود
note: Rumi gives the first line as a saying of the Prophet.

text: Knowing the harm in speech, a talker would keep silent as long as Noah lived; knowing *the harm in silence*, the silent would ask twice that to speak.
author: Abu Hafs al-Haddad
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on silence (bab al-samt)
original: لو علم الناطق ما آفة النطق لصمت إن استطاع عمر نوح ولو علم الصامت ما آفة الصمت لسأل الله تعالى ضعفي عمر نوح حتى ينطق
note: His answer when asked which is better, silence or speech. Noah was said to have lived 950 years.

text: Tongue, you are both *the fire and the harvest*: how long will you set this fire to this harvest?
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the merchant and the parrot (Ganjoor I §90, couplet 10)
original: ای زبان هم آتش و هم خرمنی / چند این آتش درین خرمن زنی

text: I looked for well-being and found it in solitude; I looked for safety and *found it in silence*.
author: Abu'l-Hasan Kharaqani
ref: reported by Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on Kharaqani
original: عافیت را طلب کردم در تنهائی یافتم و سلامت در خاموشی.

text: When words are dressed up too much, *the point is forgotten*.
author: Rumi
ref: chapter 18
original: سخن را چون بسیار آرایش می‌کنند مقصود فراموش می‌شود.

text: Speech is of two kinds, true and false. If your words are true, speaking is better than silence; if false, *silence is better than speech*.
author: Ali Hujwiri
ref: chapter on conduct in speech and silence
original: و من که علی بن عثمان الجلابی ام می گویم کلام ها بر دو گونه باشند … کلام یکی حق بود و یکی باطل … اگر کلامش به حق بود گفتارش بهتر از خاموشی و اگر باطل بود خاموشی بهتر از گفتار
note: Shortened. Hujwiri goes on: silence too is of two kinds, one full of what it has found, one merely heedless.

text: Words that come *from a heart in pain* can make a true person of whoever hears them.
author: Attar
ref: discourse 9, section 4
original: سخن کان از سر دردی درآید / کسی کان بشنود مردی برآید

text: The one who guards himself best is the one who *masters his tongue*.
author: Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on silence (bab al-samt)
original: من أصون الناس لنفسه؟ قال أملكهم للسانه
note: His answer when asked who best protects himself.

text: If you want to be honored, speak little: too many words have *made many honored men cheap*.
author: Fuzuli
ref: ghazal beginning “Bu ne sırdır kim olur her lahza yoktan var söz”, couplet 7
original: Ger çok istersen Fuzûlî izzetin az et sözü / Kim çok olmaktan kılıptır çok azîzi hâr söz
note: The poet is speaking to himself by name.

text: Be master of *your hand, your tongue*, and your loins.
author: Hacı Bektaş Veli
original: Eline, diline, beline sahip ol
note: A maxim of his order, not found in his Makalat. It is read as: do not steal, do not slander, do not stray.

text: If you see someone answering every question, telling everything they have seen and repeating all they know, *take it as proof* of their ignorance.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 65 at the source
original: من رأيته مجيبا عن كل ما سئل، ومعبرا عن كل ما شهد، وذاكرا كل ما علم، فاستدل بذلك على وجود جهله

text: What you keep hidden you can still say; *what you have said* you can never hide.
author: Jami
ref: Second Garden (on the wisdom of sages), section 5
original: کانچه داری نهفته بتوان گفت / وانچه گفتی نهفت نتوانی
note: Jami puts into verse a saying he credits to the emperor of Byzantium.

text: If your words hold no hidden truth from a heart that has suffered, *better to keep silent*, Muhammad Bakhsh, than to say them.
author: Mian Muhammad Bakhsh
ref: couplet 408
original: جس وچ گجھی رمز نہ ہووے، دردمنداں دے ہالوں ۔ / بہتر چپ محمد بخشا، سخن اجیہے نالوں ۔

text: Cleverness will not free you from people, nor selling words free you from yourself. From both, *only silence sets you free*.
author: Rumi
ref: quatrain 1670 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: از خلق ز راه تیزهوشی نرهی / وز خود ز سر سخن‌فروشی نرهی / زین هر دو اگر سخت نکوشی نرهی / از خلق و ز خود جز به خموشی نرهی

text: Lose your words but keep your deeds, and it is a blessing; lose your deeds but keep your words, and *it is a calamity*.
author: Ruwaym
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, section on the masters (entry on Ruwaym)
original: إذا رزقك الله المقال والفعال فأخذ منك المقال وأبقى عليك الفعال فإنها نعمة، وإذا أخذ منك الفعال وأبقى عليك المقال، فإنها مصيبة
note: Ruwaym goes on: lose both, and it is a punishment.

text: If you know a piece of news will hurt someone's heart, *keep silent*, and let someone else bring it.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter VIII, maxim 25
original: خبری که دانی که دلی بیازارد، تو خاموش تا دیگری بیارد.

text: Those whose very bones are steeped in love keep quiet. With a hundred thousand tongues in every pore, they *talk without a sound*.
author: Sultan Bahu
ref: bait “Ishq jinhāṅ dī haḍḍīṅ rachiā” (no. 43 in the Punjabi Kavita text)
original: عشقَ جنہاں دی ہڈیں رچیا، رہن اوہ چپ چپاتے ہو ۔ / لوں لوں دے وچ لکھ زباناں، کرن اوہ گونگی باتیں ہو ۔

text: If you want jewels, serve the wise. A fool may say a thousand words without *a grain of meaning*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: Tatcı ed., poem 5, couplet 6
original: Eğer güher isterisen hıdmet eyle âriflere / Câhil bin söz söylerise ma’nîde miskâl olmaya
note: A miskal is a tiny weight used for gold and gems.

text: Bury yourself in the earth of obscurity: *unburied seed* never ripens.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 10 at the source (11 in many editions)
original: ادفن وجودك في أرض الخمول، فما نبت مما لم يدفن لا يتم نتاجه
note: Literally: “what grows from what was not buried does not bring its yield to completion”. The Hikam is numbered a little differently from one edition to the next.

text: Wherever there is pain, the cure goes there; wherever there is low ground, water runs. If you want the water of mercy, go, *make yourself low*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book II, v. 1938–1940 (Ganjoor II §40, couplets 7–9)
original: هر کجا دردی دوا آنجا رود / هر کجا پستیست آب آنجا دود / آب رحمت بایدت رو پست شو
note: The couplet goes on: “then drink the wine of mercy and be drunk”.

text: The wise are humble; *the laden branch* bows to the ground.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter IV (on humility), section 2
original: تواضع کند هوشمند گزین / نهد شاخ پرمیوه سر بر زمین

text: To the one who strikes you, *have no hands*; to the one who curses you, have no tongue.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Dervişlik der ki bana, sen derviş olamazsın”
original: Dövene elsiz gerek, sövene dilsiz gerek
note: The couplet goes on: “a dervish must be without self-will, and you cannot be a dervish”.

text: Walk on water and you are a straw; fly through the air and you are a fly. *Win a heart*, and you will be someone.
author: Abdullah Ansari of Herat
ref: third mukhataba (on the ranks of poverty)
original: اگر بر روی آب روی خسی باشی و اگر به هوا پری مگسی باشی، دل به دست آر تا کسی باشی
note: The Persian rhymes: khasī, magasī, kasī. The Mukhatabat is a later compilation of Ansari’s sayings.

text: As far as you can, be a servant, not a sultan. Take the blows *like the ball*; do not be the mallet.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the harm of being praised (Ganjoor I §95, couplet 20)
original: تا توانی بنده شو‌، سلطان مباش / زخم کش چون گوی شو‌، چوگان مباش
note: From polo: the ball takes every stroke of the mallet.

text: Better the company of an ignorant man *not pleased with himself* than of a learned man who is pleased with himself.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 34 at the source
original: ولأن تصحب جاهلا لا يرضى عن نفسه خير لك من أن تصحب عالما يرضى عن نفسه

text: The ladder people climb is made of “I” and “we”, and in the end all fall from it. Whoever climbs higher is the greater fool: *his bones break worse*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book IV, Pharaoh and Haman (Ganjoor IV §106, couplets 27–28)
original: نردبان خلق این ما و منیست / عاقبت زین نردبان افتادنیست / هر که بالاتر رود ابله‌ترست / که استخوان او بتر خواهد شکست

text: Lord, when I look at you I am among the crowned, a crown on my head; when I look at myself I am among the humbled, *dust on my head*.
author: Abdullah Ansari of Herat
ref: Munajat-nama, prayer 83 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: الهی چون در تو نگرم از جمله تاجدارانم و تاج بر سر و چون در خود نگرم از جملهٔ خاکسارانم و خاک بر سر.
note: Dust on the head is a Persian sign of grief and abasement. The Munajat is a later gathering of Ansari’s prayers.

text: The peacock’s enemy is *its own feathers*; many a king has been killed by his own splendor.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the king and the handmaid (Ganjoor I §9, couplet 24)
original: دشمن طاووس آمد پر او / ای بسی شه را بکشته فر او

text: The wise lie low like the earth, while the ignorant *puff out their chests*.
author: Ahmed Yesevi
ref: Hikmet 14, stanza beginning “Dağ-ı hicran ezdi bağrım”
original: Dânâ tufrak nâdânlarnı köksi belend
note: Middle Turkic. The Divan-i Hikmet survives in late manuscripts and includes poems by his followers.

text: If they throw one stone at you, *bless them twice*. If they are proud with you once, be twice as humble.
author: Amir Khusrau
ref: ghazal 1583, couplet 10 (Ganjoor)
original: سنگ ار یکی زنند دعاشان دوباره گوی / کبر ار یکی کنند تواضع دوچند کن

text: Do not be proud with the poor: *treasure is always found* in ruins.
author: Awhad al-Din Kirmani
ref: chapter 8 (on blameworthy traits), quatrain 38
original: با مردم درویش تکبّر بمکن / زیرا که همیشه گنج در ویران است

text: Farid, do not scorn the dust: nothing is as great as dust. While we live it lies under our feet; when we die, *it covers us*.
author: Baba Farid
work: Shaloks in the Guru Granth Sahib
ref: Salok Sheikh Farid 17, Ang 1378
original: ਫਰੀਦਾ ਖਾਕੁ ਨ ਨਿੰਦੀਐ ਖਾਕੂ ਜੇਡੁ ਨ ਕੋਇ ॥ / ਜੀਵਦਿਆ ਪੈਰਾ ਤਲੈ ਮੁਇਆ ਉਪਰਿ ਹੋਇ ॥੧੭॥

text: Hang pride and spite on the gallows of lowliness and spare them nothing. *Let fame go*: fame has always been a plague.
author: Eşrefoğlu Rumi
ref: ghazal 4, couplet 6 (Güneş ed.)
original: Çek mezellet dârına kibr ü kine virme amân / Şöhreti ko küllî şöhret oldı âfet tâ ebed

text: Humility is to bow to the truth, follow it, and accept it *from whoever speaks it*.
author: Fudayl ibn Iyad
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on humility (bab al-khushu' wa'l-tawadu')
original: تخضع للحق وتنقاد له وتقبله ممن قاله
note: His answer when asked what humility is.

text: One walks to the Kaaba on foot, but whoever seeks the heart *must go on his face*.
author: Hacı Bektaş Veli
ref: Coşan’s modern Turkish edition (2020), p. 75
original: Kâbe’ye giden ayağıyla yürür ama gönül isteyenin yüzü üstü varması gerekir
note: The Makalat was written in Arabic; this Turkish comes from a modern edition. To go “on one’s face” is to go in utter humility.

text: A sin that leaves you *humble and in need* is better than a good deed that leaves you proud and lofty.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 84 at the source
original: فمعصية أورثت ذلا وافتقارا خير من طاعة أورثت عزا واستكبارا

text: Every good is gathered in one house, and *its only key is humility*. Every evil is gathered in another, and its only key is “I” and “mine”.
author: Jami
ref: First Garden (on the Sufi masters), section 25
original: جمع است خیرها همه در خانه و نیست / آن خانه را کلید بغیر از فروتنی / شرها بدین قیاس به یک خانه است جمع / وان را کلید نیست بجز مایی و منی
note: Jami’s verse on a saying of the early Sufi Yusuf ibn al-Husayn of Rayy.

text: The truly wise do not gather crowds around themselves; among all people, their heart should be *level with the dust*.
author: Niyazi Mısri
ref: Erdoğan ed., poem 100, couplet 5
original: Ârif oldur başına halkı dirüp cem’ eylemez / Gönli cümle halk içinde hâk ile yeksân gerek

text: Fall like a seed and you will rise to the top; do not lift your head *like the ripe ear*, or you will be brought down.
author: Nizami
ref: section 119, closing counsel
original: چو دانه گر بیفتی بر سر آیی / چو خوشه سر مکش کز پا درایی

text: No farmer sows on high ground. *Keep your head low*, so your garden turns green.
author: Rahman Baba
ref: ghazal “Kar da gulo kṛa”, couplet 7
original: دهقان کر په لوړه زمکه باندې نه کا / سرکوزي کوه چې بڼ دې مرغزار شي

text: Satan’s sickness was “I am better”, and *that same sickness* lives in every creature’s self.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the mirror brought to Joseph (Ganjoor I §149, couplet 25)
original: علت ابلیس انا خیری بدست / وین مرض در نفس هر مخلوق هست
note: Satan refused to bow to Adam, saying “I am better than he” (Quran 7:12).

text: Musk is known by its own scent, not by what the perfumer says of it. The wise are like the perfumer's case: *silent, and showing their worth*.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter VIII (on conduct in company), maxim 54
original: مشک آن است که ببوید نه آن که عطار بگوید. دانا چو طبلهٔ عطار است، خاموش و هنرنمای.
note: The maxim goes on: the fool is a war drum, loud and hollow.

text: If you argue to find the truth, it should not matter whether it comes out *on your tongue or another’s*, and you should prefer to argue in private.
author: al-Ghazali
ref: “eight things” section, first of the four things to give up (disputation)
original: أن لا تفرق بين أن ينكشف الحق على لسانك أو على لسان غيرك، والثانية: أن يكون البحث في الخلاء أحب إليك من أن يكون في الملأ
note: The two signs, he says, that you argue for the truth and not to win.

text: The palace of hope is weakly founded; *life is built on wind*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 37, opening couplet
original: بیا که قصر امل سخت سست بنیادست / بیار باده که بنیاد عمر بر بادست
note: The full line: “Come, the palace of hope is weakly founded; bring wine, for life’s foundation is on the wind.”

text: Until the cloud weeps, *how will the meadow smile*? Until the child cries, how will the milk flow?
author: Rumi
ref: Book V, the guest who soiled the bed (Ganjoor V §5, couplet 17; c. V.133–134)
original: تا نگرید ابر کی خندد چمن / تا نگرید طفل کی جوشد لبن

text: Son of Adam, you are only days: *each day that goes* takes part of you with it.
author: Hasan al-Basri
ref: reported by Abu Nu'aym al-Isfahani, Hilyat al-Awliya 2:148
original: ابن آدم إنما أنت أيام، كلما ذهب يوم ذهب بعضك
note: Hasan was an early ascetic whom the Sufis count as a forefather.

text: With every breath the world and we are made new, and we never notice, because it seems to last. Life keeps arriving *fresh, like a stream*, though in the body it looks unbroken.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the cunning of the hare (Ganjoor I §62, couplets 38–39; c. I.1142–43 in Nicholson)
original: هر نفس نو می‌شود دنیا و ما / بی‌خبر از نو شدن اندر بقا / عمر همچون جوی نو نو می‌رسد / مستمری می‌نماید در جسد

text: Come, let us be friends and make the work easy. Let us love and be loved: *the world stays with no one*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Hak cihana doludur”
original: Gelin tanış olalım, işi kolay kılalım / Sevelim sevilelim, dünya kimseye kalmaz

text: You have seen the going down; now see *the coming up*. What harm does setting do to the sun and the moon?
author: Rumi
ref: ghazal 911 (Ganjoor numbering), couplet 5
original: فروشدن چو بدیدی برآمدن بنگر / غروب شمس و قمر را چرا زیان باشد؟!
note: From a ghazal about his own death, which begins: “When my coffin goes by, do not think I grieve for this world.”

text: One thing in this world burns me to the core: those who die young, like *green wheat cut down*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Geldi geçti ömrüm benim” (Tatcı ed., poem 388, couplet 4)
original: Bu dünyede bir nesneye yanar içüm göyner özüm / Yigid iken ölenlere gök ekini biçmiş gibi

text: I died a mineral and rose a plant; died a plant and rose an animal; died an animal and became human. When was I *ever less by dying*?
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, the lover answers his critics (Ganjoor III §187, couplets 18–19)
original: از جمادی مردم و نامی شدم / وز نما مردم به حیوان برزدم / مردم از حیوانی و آدم شدم / پس چه ترسم کی ز مردن کم شدم

text: Do not be surprised that troubles come as long as you live in this world: it is only showing *its own true nature*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 22 at the source
original: لا تستغرب وقوع الأكدار ما دمت في هذه الدار، فإنها ما أبرزت إلا ما هو مستحق وصفها وواجب نعتها
note: The Arabic rhymes: akdār (troubles), dār (abode).

text: What you fear as you run from death is yourself. It is your own ugly face, *not the face of death*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, Hamza goes to battle unarmored (Ganjoor III §166, couplets 13–14)
original: آنک می‌ترسی ز مرگ اندر فرار / آن ز خود ترسانی ای جان هوش دار / روی زشت تست نه رخسار مرگ / جان تو همچون درخت و مرگ برگ
note: The couplet goes on: “your soul is like the tree, and death is its leaf”.

text: My life has gone by; alas, I woke too late. I thought *this world would last* for me.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: Tatcı ed., couplet 415
original: Ömür geçdi dirîgâ giç uyandum / Bu dünye bana bâkî kala sandum

text: Leave before you are left; *say goodbye* before you are bidden goodbye.
author: Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani
ref: session (majlis) 39, p. 162 of the Cairo edition
original: فارق قبل أن تفارق، ودع قبل أن تودع
note: From a sermon on readying yourself for death.

text: Your time is between two breaths, one gone and one not yet come. Yesterday is gone, and where is tomorrow? *Today is the day*.
author: Abu Sa'id Abu'l-Khayr
ref: reported by Muhammad ibn Munawwar, Asrar al-Tawhid, ch. 2, part 3, sayings no. 16
original: وقت تو میان دونفس است یکی گذشته و یکی ناآمده. پس گفت دی شد و فردا کو؟ روز امروز است.

text: Even when things go well, do not be proud like a branch in spring: when the autumn wind shakes you, you will find yourself *bare of leaf and fruit*.
author: Awhad al-Din Kirmani
ref: chapter 8 (on blameworthy traits), quatrain 67
original: زنهار اگرچه راست می آید کار / مغرور مشو چو شاخ در فصل بهار / چون باد خزان شاخ تو در جنباند / آنگه دانی که مفلسی از بروبار

text: In the graveyard I saw the graves of rich and poor: the poor did not go shroudless into the earth, nor did the rich *take more than one shroud*.
author: Baba Tahir
ref: quatrain 74 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: به قبرستان گذر کردم کم و بیش / بدیدم قبر دولتمند و درویش / نه درویش بی‌کفن در خاک رفته / نه دولتمند برده یک کفن بیش
note: Baba Tahir’s quatrains were passed down orally, in a local dialect; which are truly his is uncertain.

text: Wake up, stop snoring: this sleep will do you no good. One day you must leave the world, so *remember death*, and do not forget it.
author: Bulleh Shah
ref: kafi “Uth jaag ghurāṛe mār nahīn” (Wake up, stop snoring)
original: اٹھ جاگ گھراڑے مار نہیں ۔ / ایہہ سون تیرے درکار نہیں ۔ / اک روز جہانوں جانا اے … / کر چیتا مرگ وسار نہیں

text: Where are those who came here saying *“the kingdom is mine”*? Look how they lie now, turned to earth.
author: Eşrefoğlu Rumi
ref: ghazal 16, couplet 5 (Güneş ed.)
original: Kanı bunda gelenler mülk benümdür diyenler / Şimdi gör niçe anlar toprak oluben yatur

text: If you want a glory that does not pass away, *take no pride* in a glory that does.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 79 at the source
original: إن أردت أن يكون لك عزا لا يفنى، فلا تستعزن بعز يفنى

text: Cupbearer, everyone here is packing to leave. *While it still can*, let the cup go round.
author: Khwaja Mir Dard
ref: ghazal “Tohmat-e chand apne zimme dhar chale”
original: ساقیا یاں لگ رہا ہے چل چلاؤ / جب تلک بس چل سکے ساغر چلے
note: The couplet plays on chalna, which means both to leave and to keep moving.

text: Do not say “Oh, my sorrow”; say “Oh, *how little my sorrow*.” If you truly grieved, you could not draw breath.
author: Rabia al-Adawiyya
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on sorrow (bab al-huzn)
original: قل واقلة حزناه لو كنت محزونا لم يتهيأ لك أن تتنفس
note: To a man she heard sighing “Oh, my sorrow!”

text: Whoever puts their hope in the buildings of this world is *drawing a line on water*.
author: Rahman Baba
ref: ghazal “Che umeed pa imārat da de jahān ka”, couplet 1
original: چې اميد په عمارت ددې جهان کا / لکه کرښه په اوبو هسې نشان کا

text: A man had a donkey and no saddle; he found a saddle, and the wolf took the donkey. He had a jug and found water, and *the jug broke*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the king and the handmaid (Ganjoor I §2, couplets 7–8)
original: آن یکی خر داشت، پالانش نبود / یافت پالان گرگ خر را در ربود / کوزه بودش آب می‌نامد بدست / آب را چون یافت خود کوزه شکست

text: A person with a good name never dies. The truly dead are those *no one names kindly*.
author: Saadi
ref: ghazal 20 of the Mawa'iz (moral poems), closing couplet
original: سعدیا مرد نکو نام نمیرد هرگز / مرده آن است که نامش به نکویی نبرند

text: Life in this world lasts four days, so *why stay angry* with anyone? Wherever I turn, death is there; I see no one who stays.
author: Shah Hussain
ref: kafi “Dunīāṅ jīvan chār dihāṛe” (The world’s life is four days)
original: دنیاں جیون چار دہاڑے، کؤن کس نال رسے ۔ / جہ ولّ ونجاں مؤت تتے ولّ، جیون کوئی ن دسے ۔

text: The fool takes nothing from meaning and cannot sit still. He never thinks he will die, yet frets over plans for *a hundred thousand years*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: Tatcı ed., poem 80, couplet 5
original: Câhildür ma’nîden almaz oturur karârı gelmez / Ölecegini hîç sanmaz yüz bin yıllık teşvîş ider

text: Look less for water; *get thirst*, so that water springs up for you from above and below.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, v. 3212 (Ganjoor III §151, couplet 9)
original: آب کم جو تشنگی آور به دست / تا بجوشد آبت از بالا و پست

text: Knowledge without action is madness, and *action without knowledge* never happens.
author: al-Ghazali
ref: early in the letter, an “O son” (ayyuha'l-walad) paragraph
original: العلم بلا عمل جنون، والعمل بغير علم لا يكون

text: Hope is what comes with action; otherwise it is *only wishing*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 72 at the source
original: الرجاء ما قارنه عمل، وإلا فهو أمنية
note: The Hikam is numbered a little differently from one edition to the next.

text: Sufism is this: to set down what is in your head, give what is in your hand, and *not flinch* from whatever comes to you.
author: Abu Sa'id Abu'l-Khayr
ref: reported by Muhammad ibn Munawwar, Asrar al-Tawhid, ch. 2, part 3, sayings no. 13
original: صوفیی چیست؟ گفت: آنچ در سر داری بنهی و آنچ در کف داری بدهی و آنچ بر تو آید نجهی
note: Abu Sa‘id left no writings. His great-great-grandson compiled his sayings about 130 years after his death.

text: You read and write and pile up books on every side: light all around you, *darkness within*, and no knowledge of yourself.
author: Bulleh Shah
ref: kafi “Ilmon bas karin o yaar” (Enough of learning, friend)
note: Bulleh Shah’s kafis came down by word of mouth and in late copies, so the wording varies.

text: The Prophet said it out loud: trust in God, and *tie your camel’s knee*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the lion and the beasts (Ganjoor I §45, couplet 2)
original: گفت پیغامبر به آواز بلند / با توکل زانو‌ی اشتر ببند
note: A camel is hobbled by tying one foreleg bent at the knee.

text: The rarest things in our time are two: a scholar who *acts on what he knows*, and a mystic who speaks from what is real.
author: Abu'l-Husayn al-Nuri
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, section on the masters (entry on al-Nuri)
original: أعز الأشياء في زمننا شيئان عالم يعمل بعلمه، وعارف ينطق عن حقيقة

text: The Friend loves this restlessness: *effort, even in vain*, is better than sleep.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the merchant and the parrot (Ganjoor I §92, couplet 6)
original: دوست دارد یار این آشفتگی / کوشش بیهوده به از خفتگی
note: “The Friend” (yar) is God.

text: Without the journey, how can a drop become a pearl? *The first raindrop traveled*, and then the sea floor filled with pearls.
author: Attar
ref: discourse 4, opening section
original: سفر ناکرده قطره کی شود دُر‌؟ / نخستین قطره باران سفر کرد / و از آن پس قعر دریا پر گهر کرد
note: An old belief held that pearls grow from raindrops that fall into oysters.

text: Knowledge that strikes the heart *becomes a helper*; knowledge that strikes only the body becomes a burden.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, on hiding one’s state from the ignorant (Ganjoor I §156, couplet 22)
original: علم چون بر دل زند یاری شود / علم چون بر تن زند باری شود
note: The Persian rhymes: yari (a help), bari (a load).

text: Farid, why wander from forest to forest, pushing through the thorns? *God lives in the heart*: why search the wilderness?
author: Baba Farid
work: Shaloks in the Guru Granth Sahib
ref: Salok Sheikh Farid 19, Ang 1378
original: ਫਰੀਦਾ ਜੰਗਲੁ ਜੰਗਲੁ ਕਿਆ ਭਵਹਿ ਵਣਿ ਕੰਡਾ ਮੋੜੇਹਿ ॥ / ਵਸੀ ਰਬੁ ਹਿਆਲੀਐ ਜੰਗਲੁ ਕਿਆ ਢੂਢੇਹਿ ॥੧੯॥
note: Farid lived two centuries before the Guru Granth Sahib was compiled; it kept his verses in Gurmukhi script.

text: Whoever takes up a craft *without a master* becomes a laughingstock in town and village.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, Majnun and the dog of Layla’s street (Ganjoor III §17, couplet 24)
original: هر که گیرد پیشه‌ای بی‌اوستا / ریش‌خندی شد به شهر و روستا

text: I came upon a city and saw it being built, and *I too was built*, among the stone and earth.
author: Hacı Bayram Veli
ref: ilahi beginning “Çalabım bir şar yaratmış”, stanza 2
original: Nagihan bir şara vardım / Anı ben yapılır gördüm / Ben dahi bile yapıldım / Taş ve toprak arasında
note: Later the poem says: “the city they speak of is the heart.”

text: Without effort you will get nowhere on this road. If you want the wage, *serve the master*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 250 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: سعی‌نابرده در این راه به جایی نرسی / مزد اگر می‌طلبی، طاعتِ استاد بِبَر
note: The master is the spiritual guide, whom Hafez elsewhere in the poem calls the old tavern-keeper.

text: The heedless wake each morning asking what they will do; *the wise wake asking* what God will do with them.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 95 at the source
original: الغافل إذا أصبح ينظر ماذا يفعل، والعاقل إذا أصبح ينظر ماذا يفعل الله به

text: No one reached the treasure through toil, yet no one found it without toil. Not everyone who ran caught the quarry; *only those who ran* did.
author: Jami
ref: First Garden (on the Sufi masters), section 15
original: از رنج کسی به گنج وصلت نرسید / وین طرفه که بی رنج کس آن گنج ندید / هرکس که دوید گور نگرفت به دشت / لیکن نگرفت گور جز آن کس که دوید
note: Jami’s verse on a saying of the early Sufi Abu Sa‘id al-Kharraz.

text: We did not learn Sufism from talk and hearsay, but from hunger, leaving the world, and *giving up the familiar* and the pleasant.
author: Junayd of Baghdad
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, section on the masters (entry on Junayd)
original: ما أخذنا التصوف عن القيل والقال، لكن عن الجوع وترك الدنيا، وقطع المألوفات والمستحسنات

text: Be a student to one who is a master, and *you too will become* a master.
author: Kaygusuz Abdal
ref: terci-i bend 1, stanza 4 (Güzel ed.)
original: Üstâd olana şâkirdlik eyle / Üstâd olasın sen dahi üstâd

text: If the heart does not truly feel God in its own conscience, what use is learning that lives *only on the tongue*?
author: Niyazi Mısri
ref: Erdoğan ed., poem 54, couplet 5
original: Gönül duymazsa vicdân ile Allâh’ı hakîkatçe / Mücerred dildeki ilmi veyâ irfânı neylerler

text: Getting to Mecca in a day is no miracle; the desert wind does as much. The miracle is to be carried *from ignorance to understanding*.
author: Rumi
ref: chapter 25
original: یکی از اینجا به روزی یا به لحظه‌ای به کعبه رود چندان عجب و کرامات نیست، باد سموم را نیز این کرامت هست، به یک روز و به‌یک لحظه هر کجا که خواهد برود. کرامات آن باشد که ترا از حال دون به حال عالی آرد و از آنجا اینجا سفر کنی و از جهل به عقل و از جمادی به حیات.
note: Shortened. Rumi’s list ends “from the lifeless to the living”.

text: Ask whatever you do not know: *the small shame of asking* will lead you to the honor of knowing.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter VIII, maxim 78
original: بپرس هر چه ندانی که ذل پرسیدن / دلیل راه تو باشد به عز دانایی
note: The verse follows a story: asked how he became so learned, al-Ghazali said he was never ashamed to ask.

text: You turned the rosary, but your heart never turned. Milk will not set *without a starter*, Bahu, however long you boil it.
author: Sultan Bahu
ref: bait “Tasbīh pherī dil na phiriā” (no. 197 in the Punjabi Kavita text)
original: تسبیح پھیری دل نہ پھریا، کی لینا اس پھڑ کے ہو ۔ … / جاگ بناں دودھ جمدے نہ باہو، لال ہوون کڑھ کڑھ کے ہو ۔
note: The starter is the spoonful of old curd that sets new milk: for Bahu, the touch of a living teacher.

text: You can win nothing greater for yourself than to keep it busy, at every moment, *with what matters most*.
author: Yahya ibn Mu'adh
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, section on the masters (entry on Yahya ibn Mu'adh)
original: لا تربح على نفسك بشيء أجل من أن تشغلها في كل وقت بما هو أولى بها

text: Giving advice is easy; the hard part is *accepting it*.
author: al-Ghazali
ref: early in the letter, an “O son” (ayyuha'l-walad) paragraph
original: النصيحة سهلة والمشكل قبولها

text: Wipe the pictures of this world from your heart. Reach the Painter, and *never be fooled* by anything else.
author: Ümmi Sinan
ref: Bilgin ed., poem 54, couplet 6
original: Kevn ü mekânın nakşını pâk eyle gönülden / Nakkâşa iriş gayrıya aldanmagıl zinhar
note: The Painter is God, maker of every picture the world shows. Ümmi Sinan was Niyazi Mısri’s teacher.

text: The children of Adam are limbs of one another, made of one essence. When one limb aches, the others cannot rest. If you feel nothing at others' pain, you *do not deserve the name human*.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter I, story 10
original: بنی آدم اعضای یکدیگرند / که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند / چو عضوی به درد آورد روزگار / دگر عضوها را نماند قرار / تو کز محنت دیگران بی‌غمی / نشاید که نامت نهند آدمی
note: Some modern printings read “اعضای یک پیکرند” (limbs of one body).

text: Do not go about hurting anyone, and do as you please: in our law *there is no other sin*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 76 (Ganjoor numbering), couplet beginning “مباش در پی آزار”
original: مباش در پی آزار و هرچه خواهی کن / که در شریعت ما غیر از این گناهی نیست
note: Ghazal numbers differ between editions.

text: If you have *broken a heart even once*, the prayer you pray is no prayer; all seventy-two nations together could not wash your hands and face clean.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Bir kez gönül yıktın ise”
original: Bir kez gönül yıktın ise, bu kıldığın namaz değil / Yetmiş iki millet dahi elin yüzün yumaz değil
note: “Seventy-two nations” means all the peoples and sects of the world.

text: Even if you are hurt, *do not hurt*.
author: Hacı Bektaş Veli
original: İncinsen de incitme
note: A traditional saying of the order, not found in his written works.

text: Wherever you see a broken heart, *be its balm*; when the wronged are stranded on the road, keep them company.
author: Ahmed Yesevi
ref: Hikmet 1, stanza 3
original: Kayda körseng köngli sınuk merhem bolğıl / Andağ mazlum yolda kalsa hemdem bolğıl
note: Middle Turkic. The Divan-i Hikmet survives in late manuscripts and includes poems by his followers.

text: This world is a mountain and our deeds are a shout: *the echo comes back* to us.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the king and the handmaid (Ganjoor I §9, couplet 31)
original: این جهان‌، کوه است و فعل ما ندا / سوی ما آید نداها را صدا

text: Do not look on anyone as empty: *no one is empty*. The wise take no pleasure in looking at people for their faults.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Tehî görmen kimseyi” (Tatcı ed., poem 167, couplet 1)
original: Tehî görmen kimseyi, hîç kimesne boş degül / Eksükligile nazar erenlere hoş degül

text: If you see a fault in your brother, the fault you see is in you. The world is a mirror: *you see your own image* in it.
author: Rumi
ref: chapter 5
original: اگر در برادر خود عیب می‌بینی آن عیب در توست که درو می‌بینی؛ عالم همچنین آیینه است نقش خود را درو می‌بینی که المؤمن مرآة المؤمن آن عیب را از خود جدا کن زیرا آنچ ازو می‌رنجی از خود می‌رنجی.
note: Rumi adds: what pains you in him pains you in yourself.

text: A thousand friends are *too few*, and one enemy is too many.
author: Abu Sa'id Abu'l-Khayr
ref: reported by Muhammad ibn Munawwar, Asrar al-Tawhid, ch. 2, part 3, sayings no. 9
original: هزار دوست اندک بود و یک دشمن بسیار بود.

text: If anyone from Turkestan to Syria gets a thorn in their finger, it is mine. If there is grief in any heart, *that heart is mine*.
author: Abu'l-Hasan Kharaqani
ref: reported by Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on Kharaqani
original: اگراز ترکستان تا بدر شام کسی را خاری در انگشت شود آن از آن منست ... و اگر اندوهی در دلیست آن دل از آن منست.
note: Kharaqani, an unschooled farmer near Bistam, left no writings. Attar recorded his sayings nearly two centuries later.

text: It is the Prophet’s way: even to an unbeliever, *give no hurt*. God turns away from the hard heart that wounds others.
author: Ahmed Yesevi
ref: Hikmet 1, stanza beginning “Sünnet ermiş kâfir bolsa”
original: Sünnet ermiş kâfir bolsa berme âzâr / Köngli kattığ dil-âzârdın Hüdâ bizâr
note: Middle Turkic. The Divan-i Hikmet survives in late manuscripts and includes poems by his followers.

text: In the garden of this world, wise one, this is what is welcome: let no one be hurt by you, and *be hurt by no one*.
author: Erzurumlu İbrahim Hakkı
ref: verse in the section on physiognomy
original: Cihan bağında ey âkil budur makbul-i ins ü cin / Ne kimse senden incinsin ne sen bir kimseden incin

text: If someone did every kind of good but *mistreated his hen*, he would not be counted among the good.
author: Fudayl ibn Iyad
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on character (bab al-khuluq)
original: لو أن العبد أحسن الإحسان كله وكانت له دجاجة فأساء إليها لم يكن من المحسنين

text: The ease of both worlds lies in two phrases: kindness to friends, *forbearance with enemies*.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 5 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: آسایشِ دو گیتی تفسیرِ این دو حرف است / با دوستان مُرُوَّت با دشمنان مُدارا

text: In comfort and good times, everyone calls himself a friend. *A true companion* is one who sees you in trouble and shares the yoke of your grief.
author: Mian Muhammad Bakhsh
ref: couplet 4329
original: سکھاں عیشاں موجاں اندر، ہر کوئی یار کہاندا ۔ / سنگی سو جو تنگی تک کے، بنے پنجھال غماں دا ۔

text: The world has proclaimed it: whoever does wrong does it not to another's soul, but *to their own*.
author: Nizami
ref: section 119, closing counsel
original: منادی شد جهان را هر که بد کرد / نه با جان‌ِ کسی‌، با جان خود کرد

text: Sow flowers, and your own ground becomes a garden. Do not sow thorns: *they will prick your feet*.
author: Rahman Baba
ref: ghazal “Kar da gulo kṛa”, couplet 1
original: کر د ګلو کړه چې سیمه دې ګلزار شي / اغزي مه کره په پښو کې به دې خار شي

text: The rude do not only wrong themselves; they set *the whole world* on fire.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, on courtesy (Ganjoor I §4, couplet 2)
original: بی‌ادب تنها نه خود را داشت بد / بلکه آتش در همه آفاق زد
note: The word is adab: courtesy, good manners, right conduct toward others.

text: God sees, and keeps it covered; the neighbor sees nothing, and *shouts it abroad*.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter VIII, maxim 96
original: حق جل و علا می‌بیند و می‌پوشد و همسایه نمی‌بیند و می‌خروشد.

text: When fire swept Baghdad and I heard my shop was spared, I said “Thank God.” I have regretted it for thirty years: *I wanted better for myself* than for others.
author: Sari al-Saqati
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, section on the masters (entry on Sari)
original: وقع ببغداد حريق فاستقبلني رجل فقال لي: نجا حانوتك، فقلت: الحمد لله، فمنذ ثلاثين سنة أنا نادم على ما قلت: حيث أردت لنفسي خيرا مما حصل للمسلمين
note: Sari was a trader in the Baghdad market and the teacher of Junayd.

text: If they break with you, *do not break* with them: knot the thread again. If they hold on to your faults, you hold on to their virtues.
author: Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai
ref: Sur Yaman Kalyan, dastan 10, bait 10 (Bhittaipedia numbering)
original: ڇِنَنِ توءِ مَ ڇِنُ، پاءِ اُميرِي اُنِ سين، / جي اُو اَوڳُڻَ ڳِنَهَنِ اَسُونھِين، تُون ڳُڻانِي ڳِنُ، / پُٺِيءَ لَڳِي پِنُ، ھِنَ سُونھاري سَنڱ کي.
note: Latif’s image is a weaver tying a snapped thread back together.

text: Let each believer have three things from you: if you cannot help, do not harm; if you cannot gladden, do not grieve; if you cannot praise, *do not blame*.
author: Yahya ibn Mu'adh
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on backbiting (bab al-ghiba)
original: ليكن حظ المؤمن منك ثلاث خصال إن لم تنفعه فلا تضره، وإن لم تسره فلا تغمه، وإن لم تمدحه فلا تذمه

text: Never keep an evil thought in the house of your heart. Whoever digs a pit for another *falls into it himself* in the end.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Zinhâr gönül evinde” (Tatcı ed., poem 293, couplet 1)
original: Zinhâr gönül evinde tutma yavuz endîşe / Biregüyçün kuyı kazan âkıbet kendü düşe

text: Chivalry is to treat others fairly *without demanding fairness* for yourself.
author: al-Harith al-Muhasibi
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on chivalry (bab al-futuwwa)
original: الفتوة أن تنصف ولا تنتصف
note: Futuwwa, chivalry, was the Sufi ideal of generous, selfless conduct.

text: Every breath drawn in sustains life, and every breath let out refreshes the self. So *in each breath are two blessings*, and for each blessing a thanks is owed.
author: Saadi
ref: preface (dibacha), opening lines
original: هر نفسی که فرو می‌رود ممد حیات است و چون بر می‌آید مفرح ذات، پس در هر نفسی دو نعمت موجود است و بر هر نعمتی شکری واجب

text: I never complained of fate but once, when I was barefoot with no money for shoes. Then, in the mosque at Kufa, I saw a man with no feet, and *I gave thanks*.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter III (on contentment), story 18 (Ganjoor numbering; 19 in some editions)
original: هرگز از دور زمان ننالیده بودم ... مگر وقتی که پایم برهنه مانده بود و استطاعت پای‌پوشی نداشتم. به جامع کوفه در آمدم دلتنگ، یکی را دیدم که پای نداشت. سپاس نعمت حق به جای آوردم
note: Shortened. The source of the proverb “I cried because I had no shoes, until I met a man who had no feet.”

text: If this market has any profit, *the contented dervish* has it.
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 440 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: در این بازار اگر سودی‌ست با درویش خرسند است

text: Pour the sea into a jug and how much will it hold? One day's share. The greedy eye's jug is never full: *until the oyster is content*, it holds no pearl.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, v. 20–21 (Song of the Reed)
original: گر بریزی بحر را در کوزه‌ای / چند گنجد قسمت یک روزه‌ای / کوزهٔ چشم حریصان پر نشد / تا صدف قانع نشد پر در نشد

text: You are free of whatever you have given up hope of, and *a slave to whatever you crave*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 57 at the source
original: أنت حر مما أنت عنه آيس، وعبد لما أنت له طامع
note: The Hikam is numbered a little differently from one edition to the next.

text: Water inside the boat sinks it; water *under the boat* holds it up.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the lion and the beasts (Ganjoor I §50, couplet 15)
original: آب در کشتی هلاک کشتی است / آب اندر زیر کشتی پشتی است
note: Rumi is speaking of wealth: let into the heart it drowns you; kept beneath you it carries you.

text: They say so-and-so died and left his property behind. All that wealth was gathered *only until its owner died*.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: Tatcı ed., poem 124, couplet 11
original: Eydürler fülân öldi mülkile mâlı kaldı / Ol mâlun irkildügi ıssı ölinceyimiş

text: Break the chain and *be free*, my son: how long will you be a prisoner of silver and gold?
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the song of the reed (Ganjoor I §1, couplet 19)
original: بند بگسل، باش آزاد، ای پسر! / چند باشی بند سیم و بند زر

text: As long as you chase the world, the world is your sultan. When you turn your back on it, *you are its sultan*.
author: Abu'l-Hasan Kharaqani
ref: reported by Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on Kharaqani
original: تا تو طالب دنیا باشی دنیا بر تو سلطان بود وچون از وی روی بگردانی تو بروی سلطان باشی.

text: Giving thanks for a blessing is *sweeter than the blessing*.
author: Rumi
ref: Book III, the dogs who vow to build a house (Ganjoor III §132, couplet 11)
original: شکر نعمت، خوشتر از نعمت بود. / شکرباره کی سوی نعمت رود؟

text: Since all you hold will slip from your hands in the end, is it not better to give it *with your own hand*?
author: Awhad al-Din Kirmani
ref: chapter 12, quatrain 56
original: از دست چو هر چه هست خواهد رفتن / آخر نه به دست خویش دادن بهتر

text: Whoever sows *empties his granary*, but it thrives in the field. What is hoarded in the granary, the lice and mice of chance eat clean.
author: Rumi
ref: Book I, the two angels who pray for the generous (Ganjoor I §109, couplets 17–18)
original: هر که کارد گردد انبارش تهی / لیکش اندر مزرعه باشد بهی / وانک در انبار ماند و صرفه کرد / اشپش و موش حوادث پاک خورد

text: Eat your dry bread and drink cold water. Farid, when you see another’s buttered bread, do not *long for it*.
author: Baba Farid
work: Shaloks in the Guru Granth Sahib
ref: Salok Sheikh Farid 29, Ang 1379
original: ਰੁਖੀ ਸੁਖੀ ਖਾਇ ਕੈ ਠੰਢਾ ਪਾਣੀ ਪੀਉ ॥ / ਫਰੀਦਾ ਦੇਖਿ ਪਰਾਈ ਚੋਪੜੀ ਨਾ ਤਰਸਾਏ ਜੀਉ ॥੨੯॥

text: Whoever is content *is at rest* from the people of his time and stands taller than his peers.
author: Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, chapter on contentment with little (bab al-qana'a)
original: من قنع استراح من أهل زمانه واستطال على أقرانه

text: If you want such fulfillment, strive to give up your own wanting: let it go, and *you hold every wish* in your arms.
author: Fakhr al-Din Iraqi
ref: ghazal 143 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: خواهی که بیابی این چنین کام / در ترک مراد خویشتن کوش / چون ترک مراد خویش گیری / گیری همه آرزو در آغوش

text: If everyone's last bed is a handful of dust, *why raise your hall* to the skies?
author: Hafez
ref: ghazal 9 (Ganjoor numbering)
original: هر که را خوابگه آخر مشتی خاک است / گو چه حاجت که به افلاک کشی ایوان را

text: The branches of humiliation grow only *from a seed of greed*.
author: Ibn Ata Allah
ref: aphorism 55 at the source
original: ما بسقت أغصان ذل إلا على بذر طمع

text: When anything grows too dear for me, I give it up, and then it is *cheapest when it is dearest*.
author: Ibrahim ibn Adham
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, section on the masters (entry on Ibrahim ibn Adham)
original: وإذا غلا شيء علي تركته فيكون أرخص ما يكون إذ غلا
note: A verse he recited when told the price of meat had gone up. “Make it cheap,” he said: “don’t buy it.”

text: Whoever has found *the treasure of contentment* has become sultan of the land of happiness.
author: Kaygusuz Abdal
ref: poem 46, couplet 6 (Güzel ed.)
original: Kanâ’at gencini her kim ki buldu / Sa’âdet mülküne sultân olupdur

text: Do not give your heart to this world or drag your head into its quarrels: one day every deed you earn will be *weighed in the scales*.
author: Niyazi Mısri
ref: Erdoğan ed., poem 64, couplet 5
original: Gönül virme bu dünyaya başın uğratma gavgaya / Kazanduğun amel bir gün gelür mîzâna tolanur

text: For one whose only capital is contentment, *every meal and every sleep* is a form of worship.
author: Rumi
ref: quatrain 471 (Ganjoor numbering), first couplet
original: آنرا که بضاعت قناعت باشد / هرگونه که خورد و خفت  طاعت باشد

text: The narrow eye of one who loves the world is filled by one of two things: *contentment, or the grave's dust*.
author: Saadi
ref: chapter III (on contentment), story 21
original: چشمِ تنگِ دنیادوست را / یا قناعت پُر کند یا خاکِ گور
note: Saadi’s answer to a merchant who talked all night of one last trading journey before he would retire.

text: I know *a shortcut to paradise*: ask no one for anything, take nothing from anyone, and keep nothing back that you could give.
author: Sari al-Saqati
ref: reported by Qushayri, Risala, section on the masters (entry on Sari)
original: لا تسأل من أحد شيئا ولا تأخذ من أحد شيئا، ولا يكن معك شيء تعطي منه أحدا

text: The world runs on self-interest: for its own ends it bows to guru and saint. Whoever *gives up self-interest* is the lord of lords.
author: Shah Hussain
ref: kafi “Dunīāṅ tālib matlab dī” (The world is after its own ends)
original: دنیاں طالب مطلب دی وو، سچُ سن وو فقیرا ۔ / مطلب آوے مطلب جاوے، مطلب پوجے گر پیرا ۔ … / کہےَ حسین جن مطلب چھوڈیا، سو میرن سر میرا ۔

text: I do not rejoice in having, nor grieve at going without. *Your love consoles me*; it is you I need, only you.
author: Yunus Emre
ref: poem beginning “Aşkın aldı benden beni”, stanza 2
original: Ne varlığa sevinürem, ne yokluğa yirinürem / Işkunıla avınuram, bana seni gerek seni
note: Addressed to God.
